Started growing 100 avocados
TLDR: we started growing 100 avocados as a joke, but we are seriouse about it

hello avocado world

6 month ago i started growing avocado plants for fun to appreciate the growth of a plant

in this span of time i have managed to grow 7 plants, all in different stages, it was really fun to experience all of that green appearing and growing out of seemingly nowhere.

1 month ago my roommate said as a joke that i should grow a 100 plants, we cracked laughing about how it would look, we imagined how all the apartment would be an avocado forest. it got me thinking seriously.

in the following week i started to test different ways of getting a 100 avocado seeds.
i started buying a few rotten avocados from small grocery stores for cheap and sometimes for free, but it was small amounts. one day me and my friend found a grocery store that was willing to give us a box of a 100 rotten avocados for free. 

excited and returning with the treasure me and my friends got together to build the first iteration of our little farm, our top design decisions were visibility of growth, ease of execution and ease of maintenance. we had a couple of bad iteration in that day, but finally stop being sophisticated and just excuting the simple 2 toothpicks and a cup, and another 13 avocados in a closed box with paper towels. 
although we could of put all the seeds in this types of paper towel bags we decided that firstly it's important to see all the avocados easily at a glace, both for appreciation and to spot mold. 

another important aspect of the project is to measure the duration of each stage to graph the life of an avocado, each avocado has an id and every week i update each avocado in a spreadsheet with the date of each stage (split, germination, sprout, seedling), [spreadsheet link](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1ZJJfu4d4Ofo-C3omPcVUCvn7yDlpkrf3kZ2TO0f8tyY/edit?usp=drivesdk). 

as of today, 2 weeks in, we've got 37 activated avocados at once, 5 times more than i've got in six months.

the final note i have got for myself from all of this is that i actually sleep and feel better knowing there are 37 growing avocados no matter what i do, its a sort of a hack on the brain, where it can feel both productive and nonsensical.

if anyone got any suggestions for something or any creative remarks feel free, would love to get it better, we thought of buying those germination kits with watering, we also need to prepare for the potting stage. dont know if anyone will care but i will continue to update every week

Taking no shit
I’ve had my fair share of rude and entitled customers over the past 4 years, but within this last week with all the shortages we’ve had, customers are coming in hot. Just today, during my 10 hour shift we had 7 customers complain about things entirely out of our control and take it out on my crew.

One incident in particular occurred between me and a gremlin customer. Like many Chipotle’s, our truck has shorted our hot salsa so we weren’t serving it on the main line (we only have 1 inner pack to last us today and tomorrow). Well this gremlin came in and I explicitly stated we were out of our “red hot salsa” and she said okay and proceeded to give me her order. I asked if she wanted to add queso and she said no. We then approached the cold side and I asked if she’d like our mild or medium salsas and this lady stares at me with a nasty look and asks where the hot salsa is at. I once again reiterate that we’re currently out due to a shortage and asked if she’d like one of the other options. Her response back to me was that we now owed her a side of queso because of our inability to supply her with all of our ingredients.

By this point I’m irritated because she’s getting an attitude with me over something that is entirely out of my control... not to mention this being brought to her attention prior to even starting her order. So I kindly inform her that the queso would still be an additional charge. She then had the audacity to tell me I better give her the queso for free because it wasn’t her fault the trucks were having shortages. To which I responded back in a similar manner, saying it may not be her fault for the shortage but it’s her attitude’s fault for not getting free queso. 

She didn’t like that response and asked for the manager. Surprise, surprise, the manager just so happened to be me. She then told me to just put lettuce on her bowl, paid then left. 

Moral of the story, don’t be a gremlin customer :) the customer isn’t always right. Treat people with respect, it’s tough out in these streets.

Simple coq au vin, alternative version
https://imgur.com/a/oFA0qQz

1. Two frozen chicken thighs bone-in skin-off, medium onion cut into chunks, half cup each baby carrots celery sticks cut into chunks, several garlic cloves diced, 1 cup each white wine chicken base, half teaspoon each sage rosemary thyme fennel.

2. Defrost/sear chicken thighs skin side down with mirepoix uncovered medium-low heat without turning until brown.

3. Turn thighs, add remaining ingredients, simmer uncovered.

4. Done when chicken at temperature, vegetables soft, sauce thickened.

5. Serve.

Failure to thrive (Zone 9a) - over or under watering?
I’m in Sonoma County, CA (zone 9b). Last year I had a successful home garden with plenty of tomatoes, zucchini/squash, peas, potatoes, strawberries.  I did all my watering myself, which was incredibly time consuming

This year, I installed a watering system with adjustable nozzles. Evidently, I haven’t figured out how much water these plants need. I started out watering every other day, then moved to every day since it felt like everything was withering away.


Last year the zucchini and tomatoes exploded. 

Now, several of my tomato plants, my zucchini, cucumber and my peppers all look like they are yellowing, and slowly withering away. Two cucumber plants have died altogether. The tomatoes don’t look like they are growing. The weather has been mild, barely touching 80 so far this year. Google says the symptoms of over watering and underwatering are often the same. I have a hygrometer, and the soil is wet after the 6:30 am watering and then dries over the course of the day.

My question: do these plants look over or under watered? Is there something I am missing?

Best steaks I’ve ever made

My closest recipe to Japanese/ hibachi style noodles if anyone is interested. 
Japanese Style Noodles.

1lb fettuccine 
6tbsp butter salted
2tbsp olive oil
5tsp minced garlic
1/2 cup dark soy sauce
5 tablespoons brown sugar
3 tbsp oyster sauce
1/2 tsp pepper
1/2 tsp onion powder 
1/2tsp garlic powder
2tbsp apple cider vinegar 
1/12 tbsp sesame oil

1. Cook noodles Aldente
2. Sauté garlic in butter and olive oil until fragrant. Set aside
3. Mix together soy sauce oyster sauce brown sugar and apple cider vinegar set aside
4. Add noodles into wok or skillet add garlic and butter. Toss. Cook for 1 minute over medium heat.
5. Add in sauce mixture. Toss noodles. Cook for about 4 minutes over medium heat.
6. Take noodles off heat garnish with sesame oil.

I'm super proud of dinner
We have NOTHING in the house. It's been a weird grocery week, so we have some dry goods, eggs, strange freezer items, couple of sauces we usually have, and a potato. 

My husband and son had a thing tonight, so I got to putter around figuring out what dinner was going to be, and I'm ridiculously proud of it.

I made some pasta dough figuring if nothing else I could do aglio e olio and it'd be food. Chopped half an onion from the fridge and threw it in a pot to brown with the potato (also chopped). Added the last 3 cloves of garlic. Pulled a quart or so of frozen stock out, melted it, put it in the pot. Added a big spoon of chili crisp and some smoked paprika. Let it cook til it was cooked. Threw in a cup of frozen peas that had been lurking in the fridge forever. Rolled out linguine, cooked it. 

I served the linguine in bowls and poured the soup over it, and it was alarmingly good. There are no leftovers. I'd do some sautéed shredded brussels sprouts with sumac had we had any brussels sprouts. Just wanted to share.

A great pan sauce
This is a pan sauce I originally came up with for pork chops and asparagus, but it works with pretty much anything you fry in a pan. It's deep, rich and meaty.

Ingredients:

- worcestershire sauce
- balsamic vinegar (don't waste any expensive balsamico on this, cheap will do)
- molasses
- dried thyme
- garlic powder
- onion powder
- butter 

How to do it:

1. After frying whatever you've fried, deglaze the pan with water
2. Pour in worcestershire sauce, balsamic vinegar and molasses (I have no idea about the amounts, I just eyeball them, a glug of each, depends on how much sauce you want)
3. Dilute with a bit of water
4. Season with dried thyme, onion powder and garlic powder
5. Take the pan off the heat and wait until it doesn't steam anymore, then quickly melt in maybe a tablespoon or two of butter. Do it so that the natural emulsion of the butter doesn't break.
6. Pour in any juices that have come from the meat whilst it was resting.

Alternatively, you can thicken this with cornstarch.

The "base" for Indian Subcontinent recipes
So most recipes for food from the Indian subcontinent have a base that includes ginger, garlic, onions, chili and whole and ground spices.

If I look up these recipes, it seems every recipe has the order in a different way, with different justifications.

Some put the whole spices first to "roast" them and release flavour, some put the whole spices in oil to release flavour, some put the whole spices AND ground spices in oil to release flavour, some put onions first in oil and let them cook (till brown, till soft, till something, apparently they take time), then add garlic (because apparently garlic burns faster?) and then ginger, some put garlic first, some dump them all in together, some split and put some at the start and then some near the end...it's all very confusing for me.

Is there a method to this madness? Is there some proper evidence? The way I always did it was onions, ginger and garlic in the oil together, let them cook a bit, add chilli and other spices, and then whatever the remaining base was (tomatoes or coconut milk or meat or whatever). Busy weeks ahead! 8x 1 gallon bags of freezer meals for a family of 4. 
I won't have time to cook diner until January, so we're trying to out some new ideas to keep everyone full and use up the wilting veggies. Aldi had a good sale on chicken thighs and breast for ~$1.50-$2 a pound and Woodmans had meatballs for a steal. So we're budgeting on ~$8 a bag or ~$60 total.  

Disclaimer: I didn't measure ingredients or use any recipes, so these are all estimates. Measure with your soul. My family has some texture aversions, so no bell peppers or fresh onions. But they would be a solid addition. Most of these are a protein (chicken) + sheet pan veggies + different seasonings. 



Slow cooker chili: 2lbs browned ground meat, 3 cups mixed dry beans, 2 cups corn, 4 bay leaves, 3 celery stalks (I'm not sure how well they'll hold up, but they had to go), 1 large can of diced tomatoes in its own bag, a handful of chili spices (cumin, Mexican hot chili, paprika, chipotle powder), a few spoonfuls of garlic and dried onion flakes, a few spoonfuls of beef broth powder. Throw the frozen ingredients in a slow cooker for 6+ hours with enough water to cover it. Add more spice and salt as needed. 

BBQ chicken thighs and sheet pan veggies: 4 chicken thighs with the fat and extra skin trimmed, 1/2 cup of BBQ sauce, a little hot sauce, a spoonful of garlic, chipotle powder, and some fresh ground pepper all in its own bag. A mix of frozen summer squash and broccoli, a spoonful of garlic, ground pepper, and paprika. 1 large cubed, parboiled, and flash frozen sweet potato in its own bag. Seperate bags and let unthaw. Throw the meat and oiled veggies in the oven for 45-60 mins on different trays. Adjust seasoning and salt as needed. Broil chicken at the end to get a crispy skin. 

Turkey meatballs and spaghetti sauce: 1 bag of ~40 meatballs, 1 jar of desired spaghetti sauce (I use Prego garlic and herb), 1/2 cup of frozen spinach, a spoonful of garlic, and fresh ground pepper. Let unthaw and heat up. Serve with noodles. 

Lemon chicken breasts and sheet pan veggies with dill: 2 large cubed chicken breasts, a spoonful of garlic, some ground pepper all in its own bag. A bag of lemon sauce from leftover Chinese food (you could probably just use whatever citrus sauce you have on hand. Or teriyaki). A mix of frozen veggies including: broccoli, summer squash, cauliflower, brussel sprouts, and carrots. A large amount of dried dill, a spoonful of garlic, more pepper. Let unthaw. Bake veggies on a sheet with some oil, add cubed chicken about halfway through. Mix in lemon sauce at the end. Serve with rice. 

Chicken curry with naan: 2 large cubed chicken breasts with red curry paste in a separate bag. 1 jar butter chicken sauce in a separate bag. 5 naan. Frozen broccoli and 1 large, cubed sweet potato, a spoonful of garlic. Let unthaw, sautee veggies and chicken in a pot. Add sauce and a bit of water and let simmer until the veggies are soft. Optional: add coconut milk. Air fry or bake the naan. Serve with rice. 

Garlic chicken thighs and sheet pan veggies: 4 chicken thighs trimmed of fat and extra skin, some olive oil, a spoonful of garlic, some ground black pepper, paprika in its own bag. A mix of frozen veggies including: broccoli, summer squash, cauliflower, green beans, and carrots. A few spoonfuls of garlic. Some ground black pepper. Let unthaw. Throw the meat and oiled veggies in the oven for 45-60 mins on different trays. Adjust seasoning as needed. Broil chicken at the end to get crispy skin. 

Italian chicken breasts and sheet pan veggies: 2 large cubed chicken breasts. Italian seasoning, a spoonful of garlic in its own bag. A mix of frozen: broccoli, summer squash, cauliflower, and carrots. A few spoonfuls of garlic. Some ground black pepper. Let unthaw and bake veggies on a sheet with some oil, add cubed chicken about halfway through. Adjust seasoning as needed.

Healthy Avocado Breakfast Recipe
 Here's a healthy and delicious avocado breakfast recipe for you to try:

Avocado Toast with Egg and Spinach

Ingredients:

* 2 slices of whole grain bread
* 1 ripe avocado
* 2 eggs
* 1 cup of fresh spinach leaves
* Salt and pepper to taste
* Optional toppings: sliced tomatoes, feta cheese, hot sauce

Instructions:

1. Toast the bread to your desired level of crispiness.
2. While the bread is toasting, mash the ripe avocado in a bowl and add salt and pepper to taste.
3. In a separate pan, sauté the spinach leaves until they are wilted.
4. Cook the eggs to your liking (sunny-side up, scrambled, or poached).
5. Spread the mashed avocado evenly on each slice of toasted bread.
6. Top each slice of bread with the sautéed spinach leaves and a cooked egg.
7. Add any optional toppings, such as sliced tomatoes, feta cheese, or hot sauce.
8. Serve immediately and enjoy!

This breakfast recipe is a great way to start your day with healthy fats from the avocado, protein from the egg, and fiber and nutrients from the spinach and whole grain bread.

Growing onion sets for next year - advice
Im based in the south of the U.K.

My understanding of the process is

1. Plant onion seeds
2. Wait until bulbs form that are around 1/2” - 1” in diameter
3. Pull bulbs and cure
4. Plant sets in autumn or spring

In order for this to happen the following is required

1. Ground is warm enough for seeds to germinate
2. No frost within 2 months of planting seeds

I have a couple of questions

A) If I plant now I’d expect to have sets before the first frost. These would be ready by the start of October, could dry for a couple of weeks taking us to late October, then a four month wait before planting.

*Will the sets survive this long if cured and kept in a cool, dry, and dark place?*

B) I saw some references to daylight hours online but couldn’t find anything conclusive.

*Am I missing something in terms of when these can be planted?*

C) Is there anything else I’m missing? The key things I have picked up are

- it must be warm enough for germination
- there must be no frost
- it takes 6-8 weeks
- bulbs shouldn’t be too big or they will be more likely to bolt
- curing is essential for sets to survive to spring 
- not to fertilise as this can result in too much top growth at the cost of bulb development
